questions.question: What is a ResultSet in JDBC and how do you iterate it?
questions.title: JDBC ResultSet — Iterating Query Results
questions.direct_answer: A ResultSet is JDBC's representation of query results returned by a SELECT statement. It maintains a cursor positioned before the first row initially. You call rs.next() to move to each row (returns false when done), then use typed getters like rs.getString("column_name") or rs.getInt(1) to read column values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JDBC result iteration mechanics and the cursor-based navigation model
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to read column values before calling next() the first time, causing a SQLException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate both column name and column index approaches, and explain that rs.next() must be called before the first read

sections.title: Understanding ResultSet Navigation
sections.content: A **ResultSet** is JDBC's way of delivering query results to your Java application. Think of it like a **spreadsheet with a highlighter**: the highlighter (cursor) starts above the first row. Each call to **next()** moves the highlighter down one row and returns true if there's data, false when you've passed the last row. This design lets JDBC stream large result sets without loading everything into memory at once. The cursor position matters—you cannot read column values until you've moved onto a valid row. Once positioned, you extract column data using typed getter methods: **getString()** for text, **getInt()** for integers, **getDate()** for dates. You can reference columns by name (more readable) or by 1-based index (slightly faster). The ResultSet stays open until you close it explicitly or its parent Statement/Connection closes.

sections.title: Iterating a ResultSet and Reading Columns
Key Points
content: **Cursor positioning**: ResultSet starts before the first row—you must call next() before reading any data
**next() return value**: Returns true if it moved to a valid row, false when no more rows exist
**Column access**: Use getString("col_name") for readability or getInt(1) for slight performance gain (1-based indexing)
**Typed getters**: JDBC provides getInt(), getLong(), getString(), getDate(), getTimestamp()—use the right type to avoid conversion errors
**Resource management**: Always close ResultSet in try-with-resources or finally block to release database cursor resources
**Streaming design**: JDBC fetches rows in batches (fetch size) so large result sets don't exhaust memory
**Single pass default**: Standard ResultSet is TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY—you can't go backwards or jump to arbitrary rows

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A ResultSet is how JDBC gives you query results from a SELECT statement. It's basically a cursor that starts positioned before the first row. To read data, you call rs.next() which moves the cursor forward one row and returns true if there's a row to read, or false when you've gone past the last row. So the typical pattern is a while loop: while rs.next(), then inside the loop you read column values using typed getters like getString for text columns or getInt for numbers. You can reference columns either by name, like rs.getString of email, which is more readable, or by index like rs.getInt of 1, which is slightly faster but less clear. The important thing to remember is that you can't read any data until you've called next at least once, because the cursor starts before the first row. A common mistake freshers make is trying to call getString right after executeQuery without calling next first, which throws a SQLException. Also, you should always close the ResultSet when you're done, usually with try-with-resources, because each open ResultSet holds a cursor on the database server and those are limited resources. If you don't close them, you'll eventually hit cursor limit errors like ORA-01000 on Oracle databases.

questions.question: How do you check for NULL values when reading from a ResultSet?
questions.title: Checking NULL Values in JDBC ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: For primitive types, JDBC getters like getInt() or getDouble() return 0 when the database column is NULL. You must call rs.wasNull() immediately after the getter to check if the value was actually NULL. For reference types like getString(), JDBC returns Java null directly, so no wasNull() check is needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of JDBC's NULL handling quirks with primitive versus reference types
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming getInt() returning 0 means the column value is 0, not realizing it could be NULL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the wasNull() pattern clearly and mention using getObject() with casting as an alternative for nullable primitives

sections.title: JDBC NULL Handling Mechanics
sections.content: JDBC's NULL handling has a quirk you need to understand: **primitive getters cannot return null** because Java primitives don't have a null value. When you call **getInt()** on a NULL column, JDBC returns 0. When you call **getDouble()** on a NULL column, it returns 0.0. This creates ambiguity—did the database store 0 or NULL? JDBC solves this with **wasNull()**, a method you call immediately after any getter. It returns true if the last column read was NULL. For **reference types** like String, Date, or BigDecimal, the getter methods can return Java null directly, so you don't need wasNull(). This asymmetry between primitive and reference getters is a common source of bugs. If you need to distinguish between 0 and NULL for an integer column, you must check wasNull(). Alternatively, you can use **getObject()** which returns a boxed Integer (can be null) instead of a primitive int.

sections.title: Checking NULL Values with wasNull()
Key Points
content: **Primitive getter behavior**: getInt(), getDouble(), getLong() return 0/0.0/0L for NULL columns because primitives can't be null
**wasNull() pattern**: Call rs.wasNull() immediately after a primitive getter to check if the value was actually NULL
**Reference type getters**: getString(), getDate(), getTimestamp() return Java null directly for NULL columns
**Timing matters**: wasNull() checks the last column read—if you read another column before checking, you'll get the wrong result
**getObject() alternative**: Use rs.getObject("col", Integer.class) to get a nullable Integer instead of primitive int
**Common bug source**: Treating getInt() returning 0 as the actual value without checking wasNull() leads to incorrect business logic
**Best practice**: For nullable numeric columns, always use the wasNull() pattern or getObject() to avoid ambiguity

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JDBC has a quirk with NULL handling that trips up a lot of freshers. When you call getInt or getDouble on a column that's NULL in the database, JDBC can't return null because those are primitive types in Java. So it returns 0 instead. That means if you do int age equals rs.getInt of age, and the age column is NULL, you get 0. But you can't tell if it's actually 0 or if it was NULL. To solve this, you call rs.wasNull immediately after the getter. It returns true if the last value you read was NULL. So the pattern is: read the value with getInt, then immediately check wasNull, and if it's true, you know the column was NULL, not 0. For reference types like String, this isn't an issue because getString can return Java null directly. If the column is NULL, you get null back. A common mistake is forgetting to check wasNull for numeric columns and treating 0 as a real value when it's actually NULL. Another approach is to use getObject with a class parameter, like rs.getObject of age comma Integer.class, which gives you a nullable Integer object instead of a primitive int. That way null means NULL and you don't need the wasNull check. But wasNull is the classic JDBC pattern you'll see in most codebases.

questions.question: What is ResultSet TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY vs TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE?
questions.title: ResultSet Types — Forward-Only vs Scrollable
questions.direct_answer: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY is the default ResultSet type where the cursor can only move forward using next(). TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE allows bidirectional navigation with methods like previous(), first(), last(), and absolute(int row). Scrollable ResultSets consume more memory and are slower because they buffer data. Most production code uses forward-only.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of ResultSet type options and their performance implications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Attempting to call previous() or absolute() on a default TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY ResultSet, causing SQLException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY is the default and mention that pagination at the SQL level (LIMIT/OFFSET) is preferred over scrollable ResultSets

sections.title: ResultSet Scroll Types Explained
sections.content: JDBC supports three **ResultSet types** that control cursor movement. **TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY** (the default) allows only forward iteration with next()—once you pass a row, you can't go back. **TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE** and **TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE** allow bidirectional navigation: you can call previous(), first(), last(), absolute(int row), and relative(int rows). The difference between INSENSITIVE and SENSITIVE is whether the ResultSet reflects changes made by other transactions while it's open (SENSITIVE does, INSENSITIVE doesn't—though most drivers don't fully implement SENSITIVE). Scrollable ResultSets cost more: they buffer rows in memory or use database cursors that hold more server resources. For this reason, most production JDBC code uses TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY and handles pagination at the SQL level with LIMIT/OFFSET or window functions.

rows: Any direction: previous, first, last, absolute

sections.title: Choosing Between Forward-Only and Scrollable
sections.content: **Use TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY** (the default) for almost all production queries. If you're iterating rows once to build a list, map to objects, or aggregate data, forward-only is the right choice. It's faster, uses less memory, and scales to millions of rows. **Use TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE** only in rare cases where you genuinely need random access to rows—like building a desktop UI component that displays a paginated table with user-driven backward/forward navigation. Even then, modern apps usually paginate at the SQL level with LIMIT/OFFSET or use keyset pagination, which is far more efficient than scrollable ResultSets. Scrollable ResultSets were more common in legacy thick-client applications. In Spring Boot REST APIs, you'd never use them—you'd fetch a page of data with SQL and return it as JSON.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY**: default type, cursor moves forward only, most memory-efficient, suitable for 99% of use cases
**TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE**: allows previous(), absolute(), relative()—does not reflect concurrent database changes
**TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE**: theoretically reflects changes by other transactions, but most drivers don't fully support it
**Performance cost**: scrollable ResultSets buffer data and hold more database cursor state, slowing down queries
**Modern alternative**: use SQL-based pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET, ROW_NUMBER window function) instead of scrollable ResultSets
**Setting the type**: pass it to createStatement(int type, int concurrency) or prepareStatement(sql, int type, int concurrency)
**SQLException on mismatch**: calling previous() on TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY throws SQLException—always check your ResultSet type

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY is the default ResultSet type in JDBC. It means the cursor can only move forward using next. Once you've moved past a row, you can't go back to it. This is the most efficient type because JDBC can stream rows and discard them as you go, so it doesn't need to buffer anything in memory. TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE is a scrollable ResultSet, which lets you move the cursor in any direction. You can call previous to go back a row, first to jump to the start, last to jump to the end, or absolute to jump to a specific row number. The insensitive part means it won't see changes other transactions make while it's open. Scrollable ResultSets are slower and use more memory because they have to buffer the rows to support backward movement. Most drivers also keep more state on the database server for scrollable cursors. In modern production code, you almost never use scrollable ResultSets. If you need pagination, you do it in SQL with LIMIT and OFFSET or a keyset approach, which is way more efficient. Scrollable ResultSets were more common in old desktop apps where you had a table component that let users scroll up and down. A common mistake freshers make is calling previous on a default ResultSet without realizing it's forward-only, which throws a SQLException. Always stick with TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY unless you have a very specific reason to scroll, and even then, rethink your design.

questions.question: How do you map ResultSet rows to Java objects in JDBC?
questions.title: Mapping ResultSet to Java Objects in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: You iterate the ResultSet with rs.next(), read each column using typed getters like rs.getLong("id") or rs.getString("name"), then construct your Java object and set its fields. For multiple rows, you build a List in a loop. Spring's JdbcTemplate with a RowMapper lambda simplifies this pattern significantly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to translate database rows into domain objects manually, understanding the mapping boilerplate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not handling multiple rows correctly—forgetting to loop and collect into a List, or creating the object outside the loop
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the manual JDBC approach and mention Spring JdbcTemplate's RowMapper as the cleaner, production-standard solution

sections.title: Mapping ResultSet Rows to Java Objects
sections.content: Mapping **ResultSet rows to Java objects** is the bridge between your database and your application's domain model. In raw JDBC, it's a manual process: you iterate the ResultSet with a while loop, extract each column value with typed getters, then populate fields on a Java object. For multiple rows, you collect these objects into a **List**. This mapping logic is repetitive and error-prone—you have to match column names to field names, handle NULLs, and keep the mapping code in sync with schema changes. **Spring's JdbcTemplate** and other frameworks abstract this with **RowMapper**, a functional interface where you write the mapping logic once and reuse it. Modern Spring Boot apps rarely use raw JDBC for this reason—JdbcTemplate reduces boilerplate significantly. But understanding the manual approach helps you appreciate what frameworks do under the hood and gives you full control when you need it.

sections.title: Manual ResultSet to Object Mapping
Key Points
content: **Manual mapping**: Read each column with rs.getX(colName), construct your Java object, repeat for each row in a loop
**Column name matching**: Column names in SQL must match the names you pass to getters—typos cause SQLException
**NULL handling**: Check rs.wasNull() for primitives or handle null returns for reference types like getString()
**Type conversions**: Use rs.getDate().toLocalDate() to convert java.sql.Date to modern java.time types
**Collection building**: Initialize an ArrayList before the loop, add each object inside the loop—common mistake is creating the object outside
**RowMapper pattern**: Spring JdbcTemplate uses (rs, rowNum) -> new Customer(...) lambda to eliminate boilerplate
**Production standard**: Modern codebases use JdbcTemplate or JPA—raw JDBC mapping is rare but important to understand

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mapping ResultSet rows to Java objects is something you do manually in raw JDBC. The pattern is: you have a while loop with rs.next, and inside the loop you read each column using the typed getters like getLong for an id column, getString for a name column, and so on. Then you construct your Java object, maybe it's a record or a POJO, and pass those values into the constructor or setters. If you're reading multiple rows, you create an ArrayList before the loop and add each object to the list inside the loop. A common mistake is creating the object outside the loop, which means you only get one object no matter how many rows are in the ResultSet. You also have to handle NULLs properly—check wasNull for primitives or test if the String is null. Another thing to watch out for is column name typos. If you write rs.getString of email but the column is actually called e-mail with a hyphen, you get a SQLException. In production Spring Boot apps, you almost never do this manually. You'd use JdbcTemplate with a RowMapper, which is just a lambda that takes the ResultSet and row number and returns the object. That way you write the mapping logic once and JdbcTemplate handles the loop and exception handling for you. But understanding the manual approach is important because it shows you what frameworks do under the hood and gives you full control when you need to optimize something or debug a mapping issue.

questions.question: What happens if you do not close a ResultSet in JDBC?
questions.title: Consequences of Not Closing ResultSet in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: Not closing a ResultSet leaks a cursor resource on the database server. Each open cursor consumes memory on the database, and servers have cursor limits. If you hit the limit, new queries fail with errors like ORA-01000 on Oracle. Even though closing the Connection auto-closes ResultSets, you should explicitly close ResultSets in try-with-resources to avoid resource leaks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JDBC resource management and database server-side resource constraints
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming that closing the Connection is sufficient and not explicitly closing ResultSet, Statement, and Connection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention specific errors like ORA-01000 and explain that databases have finite cursor pools—show you understand server-side impact

sections.title: Resource Leaks from Unclosed ResultSets
sections.content: When you execute a query, the database server creates a **cursor**—a server-side pointer to the result set. The JDBC **ResultSet** object in your Java application is the client-side handle to that cursor. If you don't close the ResultSet, the server-side cursor remains open, consuming memory and holding locks or other resources. Database servers have **cursor limits** (e.g., Oracle's default is around 300 open cursors per session). Once you hit the limit, new queries fail with errors like **ORA-01000: maximum open cursors exceeded**. Even though JDBC auto-closes ResultSets when their parent Statement or Connection closes, **relying on this is bad practice**. If an exception occurs before you close the Connection, the ResultSet leaks. The correct approach is **try-with-resources**, which guarantees closure even if exceptions occur. This applies to ResultSet, Statement, PreparedStatement, and Connection—all are AutoCloseable and should be managed explicitly.

sections.title: Proper ResultSet Resource Management
Key Points
content: **Server-side cursor**: Each ResultSet corresponds to an open cursor on the database server consuming memory and resources
**Cursor limits**: Databases limit open cursors per session—Oracle defaults to ~300, exceeding it causes ORA-01000 errors
**Auto-close cascade**: Closing Connection auto-closes Statements, which auto-close ResultSets—but don't rely on this
**Exception safety**: Without try-with-resources, an exception before close() leaks the resource permanently
**try-with-resources**: Java 7+ feature that auto-closes AutoCloseable resources even if exceptions occur
**Closing order**: try-with-resources closes in reverse declaration order—ResultSet, then Statement, then Connection
**Production impact**: In high-traffic apps, cursor leaks cause intermittent failures and require database restarts to clear

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: If you don't close a ResultSet, you leak a cursor resource on the database server. Each ResultSet you open corresponds to a server-side cursor, which is basically a pointer to the result set that the database is holding for you. That cursor consumes memory on the database server, and databases have limits on how many cursors can be open at once. For example, Oracle's default limit is around 300 open cursors per session. If you keep opening ResultSets without closing them, you'll eventually hit that limit, and new queries will fail with an error like ORA-01000 maximum open cursors exceeded. Now, technically, if you close the Connection or Statement, it will auto-close any open ResultSets attached to it. But relying on that is bad practice because if an exception occurs before you close the Connection, the ResultSet leaks and you never clean it up. The correct approach is to use try-with-resources, which is a Java 7 feature. You declare the Connection, Statement, and ResultSet in the try parentheses, and Java automatically closes them at the end of the block, even if an exception happens. They close in reverse order—ResultSet first, then Statement, then Connection. In production apps, cursor leaks are a serious issue. If you have a high-traffic service that leaks one cursor per request, you'll run out of cursors in minutes and your app will start failing. You'd have to restart the database or the app to clear the leaked cursors. So always explicitly close your JDBC resources, preferably with try-with-resources.

questions.question: What is ResultSetMetaData and how do you use it?
questions.title: ResultSetMetaData Usage
questions.direct_answer: ResultSetMetaData provides runtime information about a ResultSet's columns: column count, column names, SQL types, nullability, and precision. You get it by calling rs.getMetaData(). It's useful when you don't know the query schema ahead of time, such as in generic reporting tools or framework code that needs to inspect arbitrary result sets.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always hardcoding column names and indices without realizing JDBC provides metadata for dynamic column access

sections.title: Understanding ResultSetMetaData
sections.content: **ResultSetMetaData** is JDBC's runtime introspection API for result sets. It lets you discover the structure of a ResultSet at runtime—how many columns, their names, their SQL types, whether they're nullable, and more. You get it by calling **rs.getMetaData()**, which returns a metadata object describing the current ResultSet. This is essential when you're writing **generic code** that doesn't know the query schema ahead of time, like a reporting tool that runs user-provided SQL, or a framework that auto-maps any query result to a Map or JSON. **getColumnCount()** tells you how many columns exist, **getColumnName(int col)** gives the name, **getColumnType(int col)** returns the SQL type constant. Indexes are 1-based. Frameworks like **Spring JdbcTemplate** and **Hibernate** use ResultSetMetaData internally to auto-detect columns and map them to Java objects. Understanding it helps you write flexible data-access code and debug mapping issues.

sections.title: Using ResultSetMetaData to Inspect Results
Key Points
content: **rs.getMetaData()**: returns a ResultSetMetaData object describing the current ResultSet's structure
**getColumnCount()**: tells you how many columns are in the result set—useful for dynamic iteration
**getColumnName(int col)**: returns the column name for the given 1-based index
**getColumnType(int col)**: returns java.sql.Types constant like Types.INTEGER or Types.VARCHAR
**1-based indexing**: ResultSetMetaData uses 1-based column indices, same as ResultSet getters
**Framework usage**: Spring JdbcTemplate and ORMs use metadata internally to auto-map columns to object fields
**Use case**: generic reporting tools, dynamic query builders, and debugging unknown query schemas

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: ResultSetMetaData is JDBC's way of letting you inspect a ResultSet's structure at runtime. You get it by calling rs.getMetaData, and it gives you information about the columns in the result set. The main methods are getColumnCount, which tells you how many columns there are, and getColumnName, which gives you the name of a specific column using a 1-based index. There's also getColumnType, which returns the SQL type as a constant from java.sql.Types, like Types.INTEGER or Types.VARCHAR. This is super useful when you're writing generic code that doesn't know the query schema ahead of time. For example, if you're building a reporting tool where users can write their own SQL queries, you can use ResultSetMetaData to figure out what columns came back and how to display them. Another common use case is in frameworks. Spring's JdbcTemplate uses ResultSetMetaData internally when it auto-maps query results to a map or a list of maps. It loops through the columns, reads their names from the metadata, and uses that to populate the map keys. ORMs like Hibernate do something similar to map table columns to entity fields. A common mistake freshers make is always hardcoding column names and never realizing JDBC provides this introspection capability. If you know about ResultSetMetaData, you can write more flexible data-access code. It's also helpful for debugging—if you're not sure what columns a query returns, you can print the metadata to see the schema at runtime.

questions.question: What is a scrollable ResultSet and when would you use one?
questions.title: Scrollable ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: A scrollable ResultSet allows forward and backward navigation through rows using methods like previous(), first(), last(), and absolute(int row). You create one by passing ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE or TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE to createStatement() or prepareStatement(). Scrollable ResultSets are rarely used in modern apps because SQL-based pagination is more efficient.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of ResultSet type options beyond the default and when scrollability is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Loading large result sets into scrollable mode instead of using SQL LIMIT/OFFSET or keyset pagination
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE and TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE, and why forward-only is the default for performance reasons

sections.title: What Are Scrollable ResultSets
sections.content: A **scrollable ResultSet** is one where you can move the cursor in any direction, not just forward. The default JDBC ResultSet is **TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY**—once you move past a row with next(), you can't go back. Scrollable ResultSets add methods like **previous()** (move back one row), **first()** (jump to the first row), **last()** (jump to the last row), **absolute(int row)** (jump to a specific row number), and **relative(int rows)** (move forward or backward by N rows). You specify the type when creating the Statement: createStatement(**ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE**, ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY). There are two scrollable types: **TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE** doesn't see changes made by other transactions after the ResultSet opens, while **TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE** theoretically does—but most JDBC drivers don't fully implement SENSITIVE. Scrollable ResultSets are slower and use more memory because they buffer rows to support backward movement.

sections.title: Step 1: Assess Navigation Requirements
sections.content: First, ask: do you truly need random access to rows, or are you just trying to implement pagination? If you need pagination, **SQL-based approaches** (LIMIT/OFFSET, window functions, keyset pagination) are far more efficient than scrollable ResultSets. Scrollable ResultSets were designed for thick-client desktop apps where a user interface component (like a table widget) lets users scroll up and down. In modern web or REST APIs, you fetch one page of data at a time with SQL, so there's no need for scrollability. If you're iterating rows to build a collection or aggregate data, forward-only is always the right choice. Only use scrollable if you have a genuine use case for jumping to arbitrary rows—like implementing a custom data viewer or a legacy integration.

sections.title: Step 2: Understand Performance Trade-offs
sections.content: Scrollable ResultSets come with a performance cost. The database driver must buffer rows (either in client memory or with server-side cursors) to support backward navigation. This means higher memory usage and slower query execution. For large result sets, a forward-only ResultSet streams rows and discards them as you go, keeping memory usage constant. A scrollable ResultSet may load all rows into memory or hold a complex cursor on the server. Most production systems paginate at the SQL level with LIMIT/OFFSET or keyset pagination (WHERE id > lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20), which is orders of magnitude faster. Scrollable ResultSets also have poor support in some drivers—TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE is rarely implemented correctly. If you decide you need scrollability, use **TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE** and test thoroughly with production-scale data.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Scrollable methods**: previous(), first(), last(), absolute(row), relative(offset)—available only on scrollable ResultSets
**TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE**: ignores changes by other transactions after the ResultSet opens—most common scrollable type
**TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE**: theoretically reflects concurrent changes, but most drivers don't implement it correctly
**Creation syntax**: createStatement(ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY)
**Performance cost**: scrollable ResultSets buffer data and use more memory—slower than forward-only
**Modern alternative**: SQL pagination with LIMIT/OFFSET or keyset pagination is faster and more scalable
**Legacy use case**: thick-client desktop apps with scrollable table components—rare in modern web/REST apps

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A scrollable ResultSet is one where you can move the cursor in any direction, not just forward. By default, JDBC gives you TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY, which means once you call next and move past a row, you can't go back to it. With a scrollable ResultSet, you get methods like previous to move back one row, first to jump to the start, last to jump to the end, and absolute to jump to a specific row number. You create a scrollable ResultSet by passing the type when you create the Statement, like createStatement of ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE comma ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY. There are two scrollable types: TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, which doesn't see changes other transactions make after you open the ResultSet, and TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE, which theoretically does see those changes. But most drivers don't implement SENSITIVE correctly, so INSENSITIVE is the safer choice. The big question is when would you actually use one. Honestly, almost never in modern apps. Scrollable ResultSets are slower and use more memory because the driver has to buffer rows to support backward movement. If you're trying to implement pagination, you should do it in SQL with LIMIT and OFFSET or keyset pagination, which is way more efficient. Scrollable ResultSets were more common in old desktop apps where you had a table widget that let users scroll up and down through data. A common mistake is loading a huge result set into scrollable mode when you really just need to paginate. Always default to TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY and only use scrollable if you have a very specific reason to jump around rows, and even then, reconsider your design.

questions.question: How do you handle null values in a JDBC ResultSet?
questions.title: Handling Nulls in ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: For primitive types, getInt() or getDouble() on a NULL column returns 0. Call rs.wasNull() immediately after to check if the value was actually NULL. For reference types like getString(), JDBC returns Java null directly. Alternatively, use rs.getObject("col", Integer.class) which returns a nullable Integer, avoiding the wasNull() check.

interviewer_intent.testing: Edge case awareness—NULL handling is a frequent source of production bugs in JDBC code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating getInt() returning 0 as the actual value without checking wasNull(), causing incorrect business logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the wasNull() pattern clearly and demonstrate understanding of the difference between primitive and reference type getters

sections.title: JDBC NULL Handling Patterns
sections.content: Handling **NULL values** in JDBC is tricky because Java primitives (int, double, long) can't be null. When you call **getInt()** on a NULL column, JDBC returns 0, not null. This creates ambiguity: is the column actually 0, or is it NULL? JDBC's solution is **wasNull()**, a method you call immediately after any getter to check if the last value read was NULL. For **reference types** like String, Date, or BigDecimal, the getter returns Java null directly, so you don't need wasNull(). This asymmetry is a common bug source. If your business logic treats 0 and NULL differently (e.g., 0 means "no orders" vs NULL means "data not collected"), you must use wasNull(). An alternative is **getObject(colName, Class<T>)**, which returns a boxed type (Integer, Double) that can be null. This avoids the wasNull() pattern but requires a cast. Most production code uses wasNull() for primitives or switches to getObject() for nullable columns.

sections.title: Handling NULL with wasNull() and getObject()
Key Points
content: **Primitive getter ambiguity**: getInt(), getLong(), getDouble() return 0/0L/0.0 for NULL—cannot return null for primitives
**wasNull() pattern**: Call rs.wasNull() immediately after a primitive getter to check if the value was NULL
**Reference type getters**: getString(), getDate(), getTimestamp() return Java null directly for NULL columns
**getObject() alternative**: rs.getObject(col, Integer.class) returns a nullable Integer, avoiding the wasNull() check
**Timing critical**: wasNull() checks the last column read—if you read another column first, you get the wrong result
**Business logic impact**: Failing to distinguish 0 from NULL can cause incorrect calculations or decisions
**Best practice**: For nullable numeric columns, always use wasNull() or getObject()—never assume 0 is meaningful

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Handling nulls in JDBC is something you have to be careful about because of how Java primitives work. When you call getInt or getDouble on a column that's NULL in the database, JDBC can't return null because int and double are primitives, not objects. So it returns 0 instead. That means if you do int count equals rs.getInt of item count, and the item count column is NULL, you get 0. But now you don't know if the column was actually 0 or if it was NULL. To solve this, you call rs.wasNull immediately after the getter. It returns true if the last value you read was NULL. So the pattern is: read the value with getInt, then immediately check wasNull, and if it's true, you know it was NULL, not 0. For reference types like String, this isn't an issue. If you call getString on a NULL column, it returns Java null directly, so you can just test if the String is null. Another approach is to use getObject with a class parameter, like rs.getObject of item count comma Integer.class. That gives you a nullable Integer object instead of a primitive int. If the column is NULL, getObject returns null. That way you don't need the wasNull check, but you have to deal with an Integer object instead of a primitive. A common mistake freshers make is treating getInt returning 0 as the actual value without checking wasNull. If your business logic cares about the difference between 0 and NULL, like 0 means no items ordered but NULL means the data wasn't collected, you'll get the wrong result. So for any nullable numeric column, always use the wasNull pattern or switch to getObject. It's one of those edge cases that causes subtle bugs if you're not aware of it.
